q: Why must adrenaline not be used in a penile block?
o: The penile arteries are end arteries
why: Vasoconstriction of end arteries risks ischaemia.

q: Which nerve is blocked in a penile block?
why: The dorsal nerve passes under the pubic ramus into Buck’s fascia.

q: During a penile block, what indicates the needle has entered the correct space?
o: A click as Buck’s fascia is breached
why: Insert either side of the suspensory ligament, advance 3–5 mm until a click, and inject 1–2 ml 0.5% bupivacaine each side.

q: Which pain scale is based on behavioural observation in young children?
why: FLACC (face, legs, activity, cry, consolability) scores 0–10; Wong–Baker FACES needs self-report.

q: Which pain scales are used in neonates?
why: Neonatal Infant Pain Scale and N-PASS.

q: After a caudal, what must be checked before day-case discharge?
o: That the child has passed urine
why: Urinary retention and leg weakness are recognised after caudal blocks.

q: Which is a recognised immediate complication of a caudal block?
o: Dural puncture or local anaesthetic toxicity

q: A 15-year-old wants to consent to treatment without a parent. What determines whether he can?
why: Under 16s can consent if they have sufficient understanding; Fraser relates specifically to contraception.

q: In England, can a person with parental responsibility override a Gillick-competent child’s refusal of treatment?
o: Yes, or the court can, if in their best interests, though this is ethically contentious
why: This differs from adult law; seek senior and legal input.

q: What is the main surgical delayed complication of circumcision?
why: Also infection and poor cosmetic result.
